chapters.title: Chapter 6: Financing Working Capital in India

lessons.title: How Banks Set Working Capital Limits: Drawing Power, Margin and Stock Statements

children.text: Two numbers govern how much you can actually borrow against your working capital, and most borrowers only watch one of them. The sanctioned limit is the ceiling written in the sanction letter. The drawing power is what that ceiling is worth this month, recalculated from the stock and receivables you declared. You can draw only the lower of the two.
This lesson covers how Indian banks arrive at the limit, how drawing power is computed every month, and why the facility shrinks exactly when the business needs it most.
Three Ways a Limit Gets Assessed

body.caption: How Indian banks size a working capital limit

cells: Turnover method, from the Nayak Committee
Micro and small borrowers, projected turnover up to ₹5 crore
Working capital need is taken at 25% of projected turnover, the bank funds 20% of turnover and the borrower brings 5%
Maximum permissible bank finance, from the Tandon Committee
Larger borrowers with full financial statements
Built from the working capital gap, with the borrower funding a defined margin
Seasonal and project businesses such as sugar, tea, construction and real estate
Month by month cash inflows and outflows, with the limit sized to the peak deficit

body.caption: Turnover method: the borrower brings 5% of turnover as margin, giving the 25% total requirement

children.text: A small unit projecting ₹12 crore of turnover is assessed at ₹3 crore of working capital need, of which the bank funds ₹2.4 crore and the borrower must bring ₹0.6 crore. The attraction of this method is that it needs one number from the borrower. Its weakness is the same thing: it assumes every business of a given size has the same cycle, which Chapter 2 showed is badly untrue.
For larger borrowers, banks work from the
maximum permissible bank finance
framework. Return to Sunrise Ceramics with current assets of ₹122 crore and non-bank current liabilities of ₹58 crore, a working capital gap of ₹64 crore.

markDefs.definition: Maximum permissible bank finance. The ceiling on working capital borrowing that a bank calculates from the borrower's current assets and other current liabilities.

body.caption: The borrower funds 25% of the gap
The borrower funds 25% of total current assets, which forces a current ratio of about 1.33
The two methods on the same balance sheet (₹ crore)

body.text: Look at the last row. Method II mechanically produces the 1.33 current ratio that Chapter 2 traced back to the Tandon Committee. The benchmark was never an abstract rule of prudence: it is simply what the arithmetic of the second method delivers.

children.text: Drawing Power: What the Limit Is Worth This Month
A sanctioned limit is not a pot of money. Each month the borrower files a stock and book debt statement, and the bank recalculates
drawing power
from it. Three adjustments matter.

markDefs.definition: Drawing power. The amount actually available to draw in a given month, recalculated from the stock and book debt statement after applying margins.

body.latex: \text{DP} = (\text{Stock} - \text{Creditors for Purchases}) \times (1 - m_s) + \text{Eligible Book Debts} \times (1 - m_d)
body.caption: Only paid-for stock counts, and each security carries a margin the bank will not fund

children.text: First, stock bought on credit is deducted, because the supplier has already funded it and the bank will not fund it twice. Second, each security carries a
margin

, commonly around 25% on stock and 40% on receivables, though the numbers vary by bank and borrower. Third, book debts older than 90 days are usually excluded entirely, along with dues from group companies.

markDefs.definition: The share of each security that the bank refuses to fund, so the borrower's own money stands first in line for any loss.

body.caption: Drawing power in a good month and a bad one (₹ crore)

cells: Available to draw, the lower of the two

body.title: Drawing power against the sanctioned limit and actual drawings (₹ crore)

children.text: Follow the two lines that matter. In October the drawing power of ₹42.9 crore exceeds the limit, so the limit binds and the borrower can draw the full ₹35 crore. By March, stock has been sold without being replaced, creditors have risen, and receivables have aged past 90 days. Drawing power falls to ₹25.8 crore while ₹33 crore is still outstanding. The account is in excess by ₹7.2 crore, and the bank will ask for it to be regularised immediately.

body.text: This is the mechanism behind the warning in Chapter 3: the facility is smallest exactly when the business is weakest. Slow sales, stretched suppliers and ageing receivables all reduce drawing power at the same time, and none of them requires the bank to take any decision at all. The limit does not need to be cut for the money to disappear.

body.label: The number to forecast monthly
body.context: Project drawing power alongside your cash forecast. A business that knows in January that March drawing power will fall below its drawings has two months to act. One that discovers it in March has none.

body.title: Compute drawing power
body.prompt: A borrower declares stock of ₹24 crore, of which ₹9 crore is unpaid to suppliers, and book debts under 90 days of ₹30 crore. The bank applies a 25% margin on stock and 40% on book debts. What is the drawing power, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Paid stock is ₹24 crore less ₹9 crore, which is ₹15 crore. After a 25% margin that contributes ₹11.25 crore. Book debts of ₹30 crore after a 40% margin contribute ₹18 crore. Drawing power is ₹29.25 crore. If the sanctioned limit is higher than that, the drawing power is what the borrower can actually use.

children.text: What Else the Sanction Brings With It

columns.label: Security and documentation
points: First charge by hypothecation over stock and book debts
Collateral security, often immovable property of the promoters
Personal guarantees of the directors or partners
Stock insured in the bank's favour, with the policy filed
Annual review, with the limit renewable rather than permanent

columns.label: Monitoring and reporting
points: Monthly stock and book debt statements, which drive drawing power
Quarterly information system statements for larger borrowers
Periodic stock audits by an external auditor for larger exposures
Inspection of premises and books by the bank
Reporting to the credit information system, with accounts overdue or in excess for 30, 60 and 90 days flagged as special mention accounts

body.title: Two rules worth knowing if your limits are large

children.text: The loan component rule. For borrowers with aggregate fund-based working capital limits of ₹150 crore and above across the banking system, the Reserve Bank requires a minimum share of the limit to be drawn as a working capital demand loan rather than as cash credit. That minimum was set at 40% from April 2019 and raised to 60% from July 2019, with the loan portion carried for a tenor of at least seven days. The intent is credit discipline: a loan has to be repaid and redrawn deliberately, while a cash credit balance can drift.

Consortium and multiple banking. Large limits are often shared between banks, either through a formal consortium with a lead bank or through multiple banking arrangements. Either way, exposures are reported centrally, and accounts overdue beyond 30, 60 and 90 days are flagged as
special mention accounts
before any classification as a non-performing asset. One bank seeing strain will not stay the only bank seeing it, so an account in excess is a system-wide signal rather than a private problem.

markDefs.definition: Special mention account. The classification a bank applies to an account overdue or in excess for up to 90 days, before it becomes a non-performing asset.

body.title: Why did the available money shrink?
body.question: A borrower with a ₹35 crore sanctioned limit finds that only ₹25.8 crore is available in March, although the bank has not reduced the limit. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The bank has quietly cancelled part of the facility
Drawing power fell, because paid stock dropped and more receivables crossed 90 days
The interest rate rose, reducing the principal available
The borrower breached a covenant in the sanction letter
body.explanation: Drawing power is recomputed from each month's stock and book debt statement. Lower paid-for stock, higher creditors and receivables ageing past 90 days all cut it, with no decision required from the bank. The limit is a ceiling; drawing power is what the ceiling is worth this month.

body.title: The binding number
body.textWithBlank: A borrower can draw the lower of the sanctioned limit and the ___ power computed from that month's stock and book debt statement.
body.explanation: Drawing power is recalculated monthly from paid stock and eligible book debts, after margins. It is the number that actually constrains borrowing, and it falls precisely when the business is under strain.

body.title: The stock statement nobody read carefully
body.scenario: A ₹40 crore limit is drawn to ₹37 crore. The March stock statement shows stock of ₹34 crore including ₹4 crore of slow-moving items, creditors for purchases of ₹19 crore, and book debts of ₹41 crore, of which ₹14 crore is over 90 days old and ₹5 crore is due from a group company. Margins are 25% on stock and 40% on book debts. The finance manager expects no problem, since total current assets of ₹75 crore comfortably exceed the drawings.
body.prompt: Compute the drawing power, explain the position, and set out what you would do in the next two weeks.
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the arithmetic. Paid stock is ₹34 crore less ₹19 crore of creditors, which is ₹15 crore, and after the 25% margin it contributes ₹11.25 crore. Eligible book debts exclude the ₹14 crore over 90 days and the ₹5 crore from the group company, leaving ₹22 crore, which after the 40% margin contributes ₹13.2 crore. Drawing power is ₹24.45 crore against drawings of ₹37 crore, so the account is in excess by ₹12.55 crore.

The finance manager's ₹75 crore of current assets is irrelevant. The bank funds paid-for stock and recent receivables, not totals, and roughly ₹19 crore of the receivable book has simply stopped counting as security.

What to do in two weeks. Talk to the bank first, before the statement is questioned, with a written plan rather than an explanation. Push collections hard on the accounts closest to crossing 90 days, since every rupee collected there restores 60 paise of drawing power, and every rupee that crosses the line removes it. Ask whether the group company dues can be settled or netted off, since that is ₹5 crore of ineligible security sitting in plain sight. Review whether the ₹4 crore of slow-moving stock should be provided against, which is honest but reduces drawing power further, so it needs to be part of the conversation rather than a surprise later.

Then fix the reporting. This position did not arise in March, it accumulated over months while nobody projected drawing power. Add it to the monthly cash forecast, because the day drawing power is forecast alongside cash, excesses stop being discoveries.

body.title: Manage the limit rather than react to it
steps: Read the sanction letter and list every margin, every exclusion and every reporting obligation.
Build a monthly drawing power projection alongside the cash forecast, using the same margins the bank applies.
Track how much of the receivable book is within 60 days of crossing the 90-day eligibility line.
Reconcile the stock statement to the books every month, since a statement that diverges from the ledger invites a stock audit.
Exclude group company dues and disputed balances yourself, rather than letting the bank find them.
Keep stock insurance current and the policy filed with the bank.
File quarterly information statements on time, because late reporting is read as a stress signal.
Start the annual renewal process two months early, with audited figures and a working capital estimate built the way Chapter 3 described.

cards.definition: The ceiling on borrowing set in the sanction letter, reviewed annually.
What that ceiling is worth this month, computed from paid stock and eligible book debts after margins.
The share of each security the bank will not fund, so the borrower's money absorbs the first loss.
The assessed ceiling under the Tandon framework, computed from the working capital gap or from total current assets.
The simplified assessment for smaller borrowers: 25% of projected turnover, with the bank funding 20% and the borrower 5%.
A charge over stock and book debts that remain in the borrower's possession.
The flag applied when an account is overdue or in excess for up to 90 days, before it becomes a non-performing asset.

body.text: Your bank limit is not the money you have. It is the ceiling on money you can have if your stock is paid for and your receivables are young. Both conditions fail together, and they fail in the month you can least afford it.

points: Banks assess working capital limits through the turnover method for small borrowers, the maximum permissible bank finance framework for larger ones, and cash budgets for seasonal businesses.
The turnover method takes the requirement at 25% of projected turnover, with the bank funding 20% and the borrower bringing 5%.

Under the Tandon framework, Method I funds 75% of the working capital gap and the stricter Method II funds 75% of current assets less other current liabilities, which mechanically produces a current ratio of about 1.33.
Drawing power is recomputed monthly from paid stock and eligible book debts after margins, and the borrower can draw only the lower of it and the sanctioned limit.
Creditors for purchases are deducted, receivables over 90 days are usually excluded, and group company dues are typically ineligible.
Drawing power falls exactly when the business is under strain, with no decision needed from the bank.
Large borrowers face a minimum loan component of 60% of the limit, and every borrower faces monthly stock statements, periodic stock audits and special mention account reporting.
